resident.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old man presented with neck pain of 6 months' duration, with paraesthesia radiating from both shoulders to the fingers, and worsening weakness in both lower extremities over 5 months.
resident.history: The patient had intermittent neck pain with paraesthesia in both shoulders radiating to the fingers, mostly during activities, for 6 months. There was no prior trauma. Over the following 5 months, the pain and paraesthesia worsened, and he developed weakness in both lower extremities. He consulted a neurosurgeon, who stated there was nerve entrapment. He underwent physiotherapy for 4 months without improvement. He then presented to our hospital. He worked as a contractor and mostly sat behind a desk. He denied any decrease in body weight or appetite and had no history of chronic cough.
resident.physical_exam: On physical examination, general condition was unremarkable (further details not documented). There was no tenderness on palpation along the midline. Examination of the cervical spine showed positive Lhermitte test, finger-escape test, grip-and-release test, Hoffman-Tromner sign, and Spurling sign. The patient was able to move his neck normally. Further examination revealed diminished motoric strength in all extremities with positive Babinski reflex and clonus, with normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. He had urinary retention and faecal incontinence. Radiographic examination showed straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter of 10 mm and a Torg ratio of 0.37. There was osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 levels with spur formation at C3 through C5. Magnetic resonance imaging showed cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 levels and spinal cord compression. Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for leukocytosis.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy, plus a likely cervical radiculopathy (C5 or C6) suggested by radicular symptoms and a positive Spurling sign.

red_flags.finding: Positive Spurling sign with paresthesias radiating from shoulders to fingers
red_flags.rationale: Indicates a radicular component in addition to myelopathy. The MRI report describes canal stenosis and cord compression but does not mention foraminal stenosis; if present, decompression should address the nerve roots as well.

red_flags.finding: Normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes despite positive Babinski reflex and clonus
red_flags.rationale: Upper motor neuron lesions typically cause hyperreflexia. Normal DTRs may reflect early myelopathy or a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, but they do not undermine the evidence of cord compression.
Not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of the myelopathy. It may indicate an unrelated infection or inflammation but does not alter the localization or indication.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The MRI report describes central canal stenosis and cord compression at C4-C5, which explains the myelopathic syndrome. However, the radicular symptoms (shoulder-to-finger paresthesias, positive Spurling sign) are not directly explained by the reported imaging; foraminal stenosis is not described.
neurology.public_message: Localization: cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy; additional radicular component suggested by Spurling sign and radiating paresthesias. Imaging-symptom match is high for the dominant myelopathic syndrome. Red flags: (1) Positive Spurling sign with radicular symptoms—changes_plan—may indicate foraminal stenosis requiring decompression of nerve roots; MRI did not describe foramina. (2) Normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus—coexisting—an atypical finding possibly due to early myelopathy or coexisting peripheral neuropathy; does not alter the main diagnosis. (3) Leukocytosis—coexisting—incidental laboratory abnormality not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of cord compression.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III; intraoperative MAP target 85 mmHg; blood loss risk low; prone position tolerance moderate; extubation difficulty unassessable because no airway assessment is documented.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or worsening of myelopathic symptoms (gait, strength, bladder/bowel function) after 6 weeks of structured conservative care.
Progression of neurological deficits on serial examination.
New or worsening cord signal change on MRI.
Development of acute urinary retention or faecal incontinence (already present; if worsens).
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the progressive myelopathy and the evidence that delay may risk irreversible cord damage. However, the patient is only 50 years old and has not had a structured, supervised conservative program with clear goals and close monitoring. I propose a formal 3-6 month course of intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and symptom control, with defined failure criteria. Success rates from structured conservative care in mild-to-moderate compressive myelopathy are around 30%, but in this case with severe myelopathy and already failed physiotherapy, that figure may be optimistic. Nevertheless, given the risks of surgery, a time-limited trial under strict supervision is a reasonable first step. If there is no improvement after 6 weeks or if neurological deficits worsen, I would accept surgery.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 50-year-old man with progressive cervical compressive myelopathy of at least 6 months' duration. The combination of bilateral upper- and lower-extremity weakness, long-tract signs (Hoffman, Babinski, clonus), Lhermitte sign, and urinary/faecal incontinence indicates severe spinal cord dysfunction. Imaging confirms C4-C5 canal stenosis with cord compression, though critical details are missing: direction and grade of compression, foraminal involvement, cord T2 signal, and dynamic stability. The patient has already failed 4 months of physiotherapy, and the deficits are progressing. In my judgement, surgical decompression is the treatment of choice; further conservative therapy is not appropriate because the risk of irreversible cord damage is high. The main open questions are surgical timing and approach, which depend on completing the pre-operative imaging assessment without unnecessary delay.
proposed_options: Option A: Proceed to surgical decompression after urgent targeted imaging (CT cervical spine with sagittal/coronal reconstructions, flexion-extension radiographs, and MRI with axial T2*/gradient-echo sequences to assess foramina and cord signal), with surgery scheduled within days.

Option B: Proceed directly to surgical decompression based on the existing MRI, choosing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C4-C5 (with foraminotomy if radicular component is confirmed intraoperatively), accepting that foraminal and cord-signal details are unknown.
Option C: Adopt the physiatrist's proposal for a structured 3-6 month conservative trial with close monitoring and defined failure criteria before considering surgery.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Option A: surgical decompression after urgent targeted imaging and then proceed to surgery within days; this balances the need for prompt intervention with the need to define the correct surgical approach.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for another 3-6 month conservative trial: this patient has severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and has already failed 4 months of physiotherapy; delaying surgery risks permanent cord damage, and the cited 30% success figure from mild-to-moderate cases is not applicable here.

I also disagree with any plan to operate solely on the current MRI without defining the neural compression: the neurologist correctly identifies that foraminal stenosis was not described and T2 cord signal is unknown; these details materially change the choice between anterior and posterior approaches and the need for foraminotomy.

The normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus are unusual and may indicate an additional process; I would like this clarified before finalising the surgical plan, but it should not delay surgery unduly.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed immediately with surgery based on the current MRI, or is it acceptable to take an extra day or two to complete CT, flexion-extension films, and foraminal/cord-signal MRI? I favour the latter, but I defer to your judgement on urgency.

Do you agree with anterior decompression and fusion at C4-C5 as the likely primary approach, or would you favour a posterior decompression given the possibility of congenital stenosis? The available imaging does not yet settle this.
Would you like me to arrange a same-day second neurological opinion regarding the reflex dissociation and leukocytosis, or should we treat those as incidental and proceed once imaging is complete?
vice_opinions.public_message: I see a 50-year-old man with severe, progressive cervical myelopathy, already failed conservative care, and sphincter involvement. I recommend expeditious surgical decompression. Before finalising the approach, we should urgently complete the missing imaging—CT, flexion-extension films, and MRI sequences that show the foramina and cord signal—rather than operating blind or delaying for another therapy trial. I am against further conservative treatment.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed to urgent surgical decompression after immediate targeted imaging; I authorize anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C4-C5 with contingencies for foraminal or instability findings. No further conservative trial.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C4-C5, with foraminotomy if foraminal stenosis is confirmed; if flexion-extension demonstrates instability or MRI shows multilevel congenital/posterior compression, convert to posterior decompression with or without fusion; maintain intraoperative MAP ≥85 mmHg, ASA III precautions, and airway assessment pre-operatively.

Obtain anaesthesia pre-operative airway assessment and optimisation

I asked Dr. Resident and Dr. Neurologist by name for their specific assessments, and they have reinforced the urgency and the need to define the compression. I accept the physiatrist's conversion and the deputy's objections: this is severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and failed conservative care, so surgery is indicated. To avoid operating blind, I order urgent imaging (CT, flexion-extension, MRI with foraminal/cord signal) to be completed within 24 hours, and I approve the operation to proceed immediately upon review of those images. The surgical plan is anterior C4-C5 decompression and fusion with contingencies for foraminal or instability findings; if imaging reveals a posterior or multilevel pattern, we will convert to posterior decompression. We will reconvene only if the imaging changes the fundamentals, otherwise proceed as planned.
